tasks.description: Set age = 20. Print 'Adult' if age is 18 or over, otherwise print 'Minor'.
tasks.hint:
An `if/else` runs different code depending on whether a condition is True or False.
`if age >= 18:` checks 'greater than or equal to 18'
If True → run the if block. If False → run the else block.
tasks.walkthrough:
`age >= 18` is `True` for 20, so the indented line under `if` runs.
The `else` block is skipped entirely. Only one branch ever runs.

tasks.description: Set num = -5. Print 'Positive', 'Negative', or 'Zero' based on its value.
tasks.hint:
`elif` means 'otherwise, if' — it lets you chain multiple conditions.
Structure: `if num > 0` → Positive, `elif num < 0` → Negative, `else` → Zero.
Python checks from top to bottom and stops at the first True condition.
tasks.walkthrough:
Three possibilities need three branches: `if`, `elif`, `else`.
Python checks `num > 0` first. It's false, so it moves on to `num < 0`, which is true, so it prints Negative and stops.
The `else` only runs when both of the others are false, which happens only for zero.

tasks.description: Set score = 85. Print the letter grade: A (>=90), B (>=80), C (>=70), D (>=60), F (below 60).
tasks.hint:
Order the `elif` branches from highest to lowest score — Python stops at the first True.
Starting with `if score >= 90` then `elif score >= 80` is correct.
If you put `>= 60` first, everything 60+ would match it and never reach A/B/C.
tasks.walkthrough:
The checks go from the highest grade down. That way, 85 fails the `>= 90` test and passes the `>= 80` test, so it gets a B.
If you wrote the `>= 60` check first, every score above 60 would be a D, because the first true branch wins.

tasks.description: Set num = 7. Print 'Even' if the number is even, otherwise print 'Odd'.
tasks.hint:
The modulo operator `%` gives the remainder after division.
`7 % 2` → `1` (odd), `8 % 2` → `0` (even).
Check: `if num % 2 == 0: print('Even') else: print('Odd')`
tasks.walkthrough:
`7 % 2` is 1, because 7 divided by 2 is 3 with 1 left over.
1 isn't equal to 0, so the condition is false and the `else` runs.

tasks.description: Set year = 2024. A leap year is divisible by 4. Print 'Leap year' or 'Not a leap year'.
tasks.hint:
Divisibility check: `year % 4 == 0` is True when year divides evenly by 4.
2024 % 4 = 0, so it is a leap year.
(Real leap year logic is more complex, but divisible-by-4 is enough for this task.)
tasks.walkthrough:
2024 divided by 4 is exactly 506, so the remainder is 0 and the condition is true.
The real leap year rule has extra cases for centuries, but divisible-by-four is what this task asks for.

tasks.description: Set temperature = 35. Print 'Hot' if above 30, 'Warm' if 20-30, 'Cool' if 10-19, 'Cold' if below 10.
tasks.hint:
Four ranges need three `elif` branches plus one final `else`.
Check the most extreme first: `if temperature > 30` → Hot.
Then `elif temperature >= 20` → Warm, `elif temperature >= 10` → Cool, `else` → Cold.
tasks.walkthrough:
Four bands need `if`, two `elif`s and an `else`.
Because the checks run top to bottom, the `elif temperature >= 20` branch is only reached when the temperature is not above 30, so it naturally covers 20 to 30.
35 is above 30, so the very first branch prints Hot.

tasks.description: Set x = 15. Print 'In range' if x is between 10 and 20 (inclusive), otherwise print 'Out of range'.
tasks.hint:
Python supports chained comparisons — very clean: `if 10 <= x <= 20`
This is equivalent to `if x >= 10 and x <= 20` but more readable.
Inclusive means 10 and 20 themselves should also pass.
tasks.walkthrough:
`10 <= x <= 20` is Python shorthand for `x >= 10 and x <= 20`.
Both ends use `<=`, so 10 and 20 themselves count as in range, which is what inclusive means.

lesson.intro:
Up to now every line of your program has run, in order, every time. Conditionals
let a program make choices: do this bit only if something is true. It's how a
program decides whether you passed, whether it's raining, whether the password matched.

sections.heading: if and else
sections.body:
An `if` line ends with a colon. The lines underneath, indented by four spaces,
only run when the condition is true. `else` catches everything that wasn't.

The indentation isn't decoration. It's how Python knows which lines belong
to the `if`.

sections.heading: Comparisons give you True or False
sections.body:
The condition after `if` is anything that works out to `True` or `False`.
The comparison operators are `==` equal, `!=` not equal, `<`, `>`, `<=` and `>=`.

Notice that equality is two equals signs. One `=` assigns a value.

sections.heading: More than two options with elif
sections.body:
`elif` is short for "else if". Python checks each condition from the top and
runs the first one that's true, then skips the rest. Order matters for that
reason: put the most specific check first.

sections.heading: Combining conditions
sections.body:
`and` needs both sides true. `or` needs at least one. `not` flips it.
For "is x between two values", Python lets you chain comparisons, which reads
nicely: `10 <= x <= 20`.
sections.code:
x = 15
if 10 <= x <= 20:
    print('In range')

raining = False
cold = True
if raining or cold:
    print('Take a coat')

sections.heading: The remainder trick
sections.body:
`%` gives the remainder of a division. `7 % 2` is `1`, `8 % 2` is `0`.
So `n % 2 == 0` means "n is even", and `year % 4 == 0` means "divisible by 4".
You'll use this constantly.

watch_out: Missing the colon at the end of the `if`, `elif` or `else` line.
Writing `if x = 5:` with one equals sign. Comparing needs `==`.
Forgetting to indent the lines under the `if`. Python will tell you it expected an indented block.
Checking ranges in the wrong order. If you test `score >= 60` before `score >= 90`, a score of 95 gets caught by the first one.
